global.statement: With both coefficients free and at least one positive count, a finite MLE exists and is unique if and only if $S^2>\bar x$, where $S^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$. Otherwise the supremum is the Poisson limit. For all-zero data, the maximum is attained by every pair with $r=0$ or $p=1$, so the coefficients are not unique. With $r>0$ held, the free probability has a unique MLE, including $p=1$ for all-zero data. With $0<p<1$ held, the free size has a unique MLE, including $r=0$ for all-zero data. Held $r=0$ or $p=1$ permits only zeros and leaves the other free coefficient unidentified. Holding both coefficients leaves only likelihood evaluation.
global.reason: The free-fit criterion and uniqueness for positive-mean samples are proved below by expanding the convexity argument of Brøns and Jensen (1988), including strictness and the equality case. Levin and Reeds (1977) is the classical published reference; its proof was not accessible in this check. Aragón, Eberly and Eberly (1992) is not used as a proof authority because Wang (1996) reports an error in its argument. For held positive size, maximizing in probability gives $p=r/(r+\bar x)$. For held $0<p<1$, the size score is $n\log p+\sum_i\sum_{j=0}^{x_i-1}(r+j)^{-1}$. If some count is positive, it decreases strictly from infinity to $n\log p<0$, so it has one root. If all counts vanish, the likelihood is $p^{nr}$ and its maximum is attained at $r=0$.
